chunks: "The gate of a MOSFET looks like a capacitor, a nanofarad or so, and the wire to it, the bond wires, the package lead and the trace, has inductance, maybe 10 to 30 nanohenries.
A driver with a stiff, fast edge feeding an inductor into a capacitor is a series LC circuit.
If there's no resistance in it, it rings, and the ringing frequency is one over two pi root LC, around 35 megahertz for 20 nanohenries and a nanofarad.
The gate voltage overshoots well above the drive voltage, maybe 70% for a lightly damped loop, so a 3.
3 volt drive could see over 5 volts, and with a 12 volt driver you can approach the gate rating.
That ringing can also turn the FET on and off repeatedly, which is parasitic oscillation.
Parasitic oscillation more broadly is when the FET, with its feedback through the gate-drain capacitance and the source inductance, forms an unintended oscillator at tens or hundreds of megahertz.
It's especially common when the FET is in its linear region, or when several FETs are paralleled with a shared gate wire. The series resistor attacks all of that.
It adds damping: with enough resistance, R at least 2 square root of L over C , about 9 ohms here, the response is critically damped with no overshoot.
It limits the peak current out of the GPIO, since a microcontroller pin can only give 10 or 20 milliamps. And it slows the edge, which reduces dv/dt, EMI and Miller coupling.
The price is slower switching: more resistance means longer transitions and more switching loss, so I'd pick the smallest value that gives a clean gate waveform and current within the pin limit."
